options: Some orders made to order, some from stock

questions.text: How do you track an order from enquiry to dispatch?
questions.ideal: Every order tracked in one system, from enquiry to dispatch

questions.text: How many Excel sheets does your team update every week?
questions.ideal: Five sheets or fewer; everything else lives in one system

questions.text: How often do delivery dates slip, or stock surprise you?
questions.ideal: Dates rarely slip, and stock rarely surprises

questions.text: A customer asks “Where is my order?” How long does it take to answer?
questions.ideal: Anyone in the team can answer in under a minute

questions.text: How quickly can you see today’s sales, dues and stock?
options: Only when the accountant prepares it
questions.ideal: Sales, dues and stock visible live, any time

questions.text: If a figure is changed, can you see who changed it and when?
questions.ideal: Every change recorded with name, date and time

questions.text: What are your biggest headaches right now?

firefighting: Your business runs on people’s effort and memory. It works, but it is tiring, and it limits how fast you can grow.
partly: Some systems are in place, but the gaps between them still cost time and bring surprises.
in_control: You have a good grip. The gains from here are in fine-tuning and visibility.

q2: Put every order on one screen
When orders live in Excel and WhatsApp, the latest status sits in someone’s head. One screen from enquiry to dispatch lets anyone see where an order stands.
Sales, work orders and dispatch in one place, with promised and actual dates.
q3: Retire the spreadsheets one by one
Every extra sheet is another version of the truth, and someone’s evening spent matching them up. Start with the sheet that is updated most often.
Orders, stock, purchase and production in one system, so the sheets are no longer needed.
q4: Plan against real capacity and stock
Most slipped dates are promised before anyone checks machines and material. Check both before a date is given.
Production planning and material readiness for every work order, with Predictive & order outlook.
q5: Answer “Where is my order?” in seconds
If the answer needs three phone calls, the customer feels it. Give everyone the same live status.
Live order and dispatch status, with dispatch release sign-off.
q6: Decisions made on last month’s figures are guesses. A short daily look at sales, dues and stock changes how the week is run.
Live views of sales, receivables, payables and stock.
q7: Know who changed what, and when
When a figure changes without a trace, trust goes with it. A record of every change settles questions in minutes.
An audit log of every change, with roles and approvals.
h_dispatch: Fix a daily dispatch plan from confirmed stock, and release only what is checked and packed.
Dispatch controls with release sign-off, delivery challans and invoices.
h_stock: Make stock figures match the shelf
Record every issue and receipt when it happens, and count a few items every week instead of everything once a year.
Stores with bin cards, issues against work orders, stock counts and reorder alerts.
h_planning: Plan the week before it starts
A simple weekly plan by machine and order, reviewed every morning, removes most of the daily firefighting.
Production planning, job cards and machine efficiency (OEE).
h_cash: Review dues every week, oldest first, and note every promise to pay. Small habits shorten the cash cycle.
A collection worklist, ageing, promises to pay and a weekly cash-flow view.
h_accountability: Give every order and task a named owner and a date. Visible ownership does more than reminders.
Roles, approvals and each person’s own work list, with an audit log.
h_quality: Catch problems before the customer does
Inspect at receipt, during production and before dispatch, and record every rejection with its reason. Patterns show up quickly.
Inspections, test certificates and an NCR / CAPA register.
h_tenders: Keep every enquiry, quotation and tender in one list with its due date and next step, and review it weekly.
A tender and quotation pipeline with due dates, follow-ups and win rates.

q2: List every open order in one place, with customer, promised date and current stage.
Update that list every day at a fixed time, and stop tracking orders in personal sheets and chats.
Review late orders every week and agree one owner and a new date for each.
q3: List every sheet the team updates, and who owns each one.
Pick the two sheets updated most often and move them into one shared system.
Count the sheets again. Aim for a third fewer, and keep going.
q4: Before promising any date this week, check machine load and material for that order.
Keep a simple weekly load view by machine or work centre, with a shortage list.
Compare promised and actual dates for the month, and find the two biggest causes of slips.
q5: Agree the stages every order passes through, from order to dispatch.
Record each order’s stage as it moves, in one place everyone can see.
Test it: pick five orders at random and check that anyone can answer in under a minute.
q6: Choose the five numbers you want every day: sales, dues, collections, stock and pending dispatch.
Have them updated every evening, even by hand at first.
Start each morning with a 10-minute look, and take one decision from it.
q7: Note the figures that matter most: prices, stock, dispatch quantities and payments.
Limit who can change them, and keep a record of every change with name and time.
Review the record of changes once a week for anything unexpected.
h_dispatch: Make the dispatch plan each morning from stock that is ready, not stock expected.
Add a final check before release: quantity, packing and documents.
Track on-time dispatches for the month and fix the most common delay.
h_stock: Record every issue and receipt on the same day, with a reason for any adjustment.
Count ten fast-moving items every week and correct the differences.
Set reorder levels for the items that ran out this month.
h_planning: Hold a 15-minute planning meeting every morning, by machine and order.
Make next week’s plan before Friday and share it with the shop floor.
Compare plan and actual every week, and adjust the next plan.
h_cash: List every customer due, oldest first, with amount and promised date.
Call the top ten every week and note each promise to pay.
Every Monday, look at the money coming in and going out over the next four weeks.
h_accountability: Give every open order and task one named owner and a due date.
Make each person’s list visible to them and their manager.
Review overdue items every week, by owner, without blame.
h_quality: Record every rejection with item, quantity and reason.
Add a simple check at receipt and before dispatch.
Look at the top three rejection reasons and act on the biggest one.
h_tenders: Put every open enquiry, quotation and tender in one list, with its due date.
Add the next step and an owner for each, and review the list twice a week.
Count wins and losses for the month, and note why each one was lost.
